description: The preliminary selection of outdoor units in multi-split air conditioning systems requires more than a comparison between indoor and outdoor nominal cooling power. description: This article presents a calculation tool developed to support decision-making based on a technical-economic analysis for the replacement of air-conditioning and domestic hot water systems. Evaluation of the proposed architecture confirms its economic advantages over traditional hardware smart meters, specifically demonstrating a drastic reduction in deployment time and minimized capital investments. description:
With the growing need to decarbonize the electricity sector, it is essential to maximize the use of renewable energy. The concept developed consists of a solution for storing high-temperature thermal energy by using surplus electricity from renewable sources. The main goal is to investigate the potential Thermal Energy Storage (TES) using natural rocks as solid medium, specifically basalt, due to its abundance and low cost, and air as the heat transfer fluid. 
During the charging process, high-temperature heat is generated by an electric resistance, after which the heated air enters the packed bed at the bottom. In this stage, it is considered internal recirculation of the air. For the discharge, two flow orientations are investigated: 1) same direction as for charging stage, where cold air enters the system at the bottom and is extracted at the top; 2) flow direction reversed with respect to charging flow direction. 
A simplified one-dimensional numerical model based on a porous medium approach is considered to analyse the temperature evolution of the packed bed. For validation, a CFD simulation is carried out, where it is considered a porous medium under a local thermal equilibrium basis, and the porous inertial and viscous resistances are calculated according to the Ergun equation.
Based on the simplified model, parametric studies are carried out to identify critical parameters for optimal system operation, such as maximum and minimum temperatures of the packed bed, the air flow rate for the internal recirculation on the charging stage, and the duration of the charging and discharging stages, as well as input power variations throughout the day according to solar Photo-Voltaic (PV) power generation.

description: Doubly fed induction generator remains the dominant choice for most variable-speed wind energy conversion configurations, the reduced converter rating and independent active and reactive power control are the leading motivations. The machine alone cannot operate properly, the rotor side converter handles the slip power and lets the turbine generate power above or below its synchronous speed. However the RSC is still conventionally implemented as a hard switched two level voltage source inverter. This approach leads to multiple switching losses that scale with the slip frequency, including dc-bus voltage and rotor current ripples, that become proportionally more costly when the turbine is bigger with more compact nacelle mounted power electronics. Auxiliary resonant commutated pole inverters, z-source inverters, and active clamp resonant converters have each been independently proposed as soft switching alternatives to mitigate these losses. However no controlled study has yet benchmarked them one against the other, or against the conventional hard switched baseline, under a common DFIG model and wind profile.This paper compares four RSC topologies, hard switched two level VSI, ARCP-VSI, Z-source inverter, and active clamp resonant converter, are implemented on the same DFIG turbine model and run through the same variable wind speed profile and grid fault scenarios. The control law is kept identical across all four, stator flux oriented vector control with MPPT, so the compared results can be traced back to the converter topology. Switching loss, overall efficiency, rotor current THD and the dynamic response during slip transitions and low voltage ride through events are all tracked the same way for each topology. The goal is twofold, first to find which soft switching topology gives the best efficiency to complexity trade off across the full slip range of a modern multi megawatt DFIG turbine, and second to check the efficiency gains reported across all four topologies.

description: Achieving sustainability is the greatest challenge humanity currently faces. The future of humanity and planet Earth depends on it. Given this challenge, it is essential to reduce the consumption of energy and other natural resources, as well as to produce less waste of materials. Given the high number of buildings and the corresponding widespread use of electrical installations necessary for the distribution of low-voltage electricity, these deserve particular attention and study of their impact on sustainability. In this context, and aligned with the need to promote sustainability, the present study aimed to analyse the results obtained by the proposal identified in the literature for improving the sizing of cables in electrical installations. The identified and analysed proposal aims to increase the availability of standardized cross-sections in order to increase the current density in conductors. According to the identified proposal (the "micro system approach" method), this minimizes the waste of resources (especially copper) and reduces economic costs and environmental impact. The results of the study show that decreasing the cross-section increases the operating temperature of the conductor, which reduces its lifespan. This could have impacts on resource use, since if the installation has a projected lifespan longer than the conductor's lifespan, the conductor will have to be replaced during the installation's lifetime; which entails additional investment costs and greater use of copper. Thus, the results show that it is not clear whether reducing copper use will translate into economic savings or a reduction in copper use in the long term. The results also show that there is a global increase in CO2 emissions due to increased Joule losses. These results highlight the importance of evaluating technical proposals from a comprehensive perspective, not restricted to a single aspect, when analysing the impact of a new technological proposal on sustainability.

Wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) consume large amounts of electricity, while many existing anaerobic digestion systems operate below their design energy capacity. Improving the performance of these facilities is essential for increasing energy self-sufficiency and supporting low-carbon wastewater treatment.
This study proposes an engineering framework for improving the energy efficiency of existing WWTPs using the Durres Wastewater Treatment Plant (Albania) as a case study. These interventions address the critical process bottlenecks limiting biogas recovery and electricity generation while avoiding major infrastructure reconstruction.
The study demonstrates that upgrading process efficiency rather than replacing treatment infrastructure offers a practical pathway to increase renewable energy recovery, improve plant energy self-sufficiency, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. description:
Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning (HVAC) systems, where centrifugal fans are widely used, represent a relevant electricity consumption in buildings sector, that will increase due to a higher thermal comfort demand associated to climate change and higher indoor air quality requirements. Variable speed drives to adjust the fan speed in part-load operation is a well-known and recommended technology to reduce energy consumption. 
This work presents an experimental assessment of a centrifugal fan operating under variable speed conditions representative of HVAC applications in non‑residential buildings. Tests were conducted at three operating frequencies (50, 40 and 30 Hz), allowing the analysis of the influence of rotational speed on the aerodynamic performance and on the electrical energy consumption of the fan.
The results show that reducing the operating frequency leads to a decrease in airflow rate, pressure rise and also decrease electrical power consumption, confirming the dependence of the fan performance on the rotational speed. The characteristic curves follow the expected aerodynamic behavior, while the analysis of useful power and efficiency highlights the influence of operating conditions on overall performance. A comparison between valve‑controlled and speed‑controlled operation was also performed. Reductions between 22% and 56% of electric power consumption was observed with airflow rates variation from 80% to 30% (of nominal airflow rate) which are representative of typical part-load operation in HVAC systems. These results highlight that variable speed operation has an important effect on the fan’s energy efficiency compared to traditional throttling methods. 
The findings enhance that variable speed drives increase operational flexibility of ventilation systems and contributes to reduce its energy consumption in real HVAC applications.

description:
Buildings are among the largest consumers of energy worldwide and represent a significant source of greenhouse gas emissions. Improving their energy performance is therefore essential to achieving climate and decarbonisation targets. In this context, energy certification has become an important tool for evaluating building performance, identifying improvement opportunities, and supporting investment decisions that reduce energy use and operating costs.

This study presents the energy assessment and certification of a hotel building in Portugal under the Portuguese Energy Certification System. The work included an on-site energy audit, detailed characterisation of the building envelope and technical systems, and dynamic energy simulation to determine current energy performance and estimate the impact of different retrofit measures. Particular attention was given to the thermal behaviour of the building envelope, HVAC systems, domestic hot water production, and electricity consumption.

The assessment showed that the building currently holds an energy rating of class C, revealing substantial potential for improvement. Three retrofit measures were evaluated: a photovoltaic self-consumption system, improved roof thermal insulation, and the replacement of existing gas boilers with a high-efficiency condensing boiler. The photovoltaic system and roof insulation delivered the best balance between energy savings and economic performance, reducing annual energy consumption by 10.6% and 13.6%, respectively, and improving the energy rating from class C to B−. Their simple payback periods were estimated at 5.6 and 8.5 years. When implemented together, these measures reduced total annual energy consumption by 26.2%, corresponding to annual savings of approximately €9,200 and an overall payback period of 8.6 years.

These findings demonstrate that energy certification provides an effective decision-support framework for the hospitality sector, enabling stakeholders to identify technically feasible and economically attractive retrofit solutions while supporting lower energy consumption, reduced operating costs, lower carbon emissions, and more sustainable building management.
title: Energy Performance Assessment and Cost-Effective Retrofit Measures for a Hotel Building: A Portuguese Case Study

description:
Quantifying the contribution of renewable energy sources to greenhouse gas emission reductions requires methodologies that consider not only the replacement of conventional electricity generation but also the broader effects of renewable integration on power system operation. Conventional approaches generally estimate avoided emissions by accounting only for the displacement of fossil-fuel-based generation, overlooking the impact of renewable generation on network losses.

This paper presents a methodology for estimating avoided CO₂ emissions in electrical power systems that explicitly incorporates the influence of network topology and the voltage level at which renewable generation is connected. Moreover, the proposed approach quantifies the reduction in transmission and distribution losses resulting from the integration of distributed renewable energy resources.

The methodology is applied to the Portuguese Electrical Power System using long-term development scenarios extending to 2050. The analysis combines electricity demand projections with expected renewable generation expansion to estimate cumulative avoided emissions under different decarbonisation pathways. Particular attention is given to the location of distributed generation within the network and its influence on loss reduction and overall environmental performance. The results show that considering avoided network losses provides a more comprehensive assessment of the environmental benefits of renewable energy deployment. For the Portuguese case study, cumulative avoided emissions between 2023 and 2050 are estimated to range from 214 MtCO₂ to 267 MtCO₂, depending on assumptions regarding electricity demand growth and renewable energy expansion. The analysis also demonstrates that network topology and the distribution of renewable generation across voltage levels significantly affect the estimated emission reductions.

Overall, the proposed methodology offers a practical framework for assessing the climate benefits of renewable energy integration. By accounting for both generation displacement and reductions in network losses, it provides valuable support for planning, regulatory, and policy decisions aimed at accelerating the transition towards carbon-neutral electricity systems.
title: Towards More Accurate Carbon Accounting in Power Systems: Incorporating Network Losses into Renewable Energy Assessments —Application to the Portuguese Electricity System

description: Cellulose nanocrystals (CNC) are increasing attention in engineering due to their biocompatibility, biodegradability, and excellent mechanical properties. This work focuses on the manufacturing and technical characterisation of Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) parts reinforced with various CNC loads using fused filament fabrication (FFF - 3D printing). To ensure functional composite filaments, a powder-based dry-mixing methodology is implemented, using both a commercial ultra-fine PLA matrix and a laboratory wet-milled PLA matrix processed through an intermittent 10-cycle high-power shredding protocol. Due to the high hygroscopic character and thus moisture sensitivity of both components, all mixture formulations undergo continuous dehydration at 50 °C for at least four hours prior to single-screw melt extrusion. Quality control during compounding is systematically monitored via integrated optical diameter sensors, maintaining strict geometric tolerances of 1.75 ± 0.05 mm, which prevents sub-extrusion and void generation during deposition. Uniaxial tensile tests on the pure PLA matrix established that post-printing physical ageing critically influences mechanical repeatability. Cross-examination of the resulting stress-strain curves demonstrated that a 24-hour post-printing window provides the optimal performance, minimizing data dispersion for maximum tensile strength (SD ~ 1.24 MPa) and establishing a reliable analytical baseline. Ongoing work processes composite formulations with loads of 1 and 2 wt% CNC. Based on the shear-induced fiber alignment and the strong nucleating effect reported in the literature, the homogeneous dispersion of shear aligned nanoparticles is expected to accelerate matrix crystallization, resulting in a substantial increase in Young's modulus and overall structural performance.

description: Domestic hot water production accounts for a significant share of energy use in residential and service buildings, and its costs are affected by renewable heat availability and electricity price fluctuations. This paper describes a low-cost controller for integrated thermal energy systems for domestic hot water. The prototype manages multiple heat sources: a solar thermal collector, an electric resistance heater, and either a biomass boiler or a heat pump. The controller runs on a Raspberry Pi and uses DS18B20 temperature sensors with a relay module to monitor storage tank supply and return temperatures and actuate equipment. A touchscreen interface allows configuration of limits, setpoints, hysteresis bands, tariffs, fuel parameters, and heat-source traits. The control strategy prioritises solar thermal energy when available or forecasted, while auxiliary sources are chosen based on estimated production costs. The algorithm uses weather forecasts and electricity prices, including fixed or indexed tariffs, to minimize expensive operation and capitalize on lower-cost periods for heating. For pellet boiler systems, the controller compares boiler thermal cost with resistance heating cost and only uses the boiler when operating conditions favor effective heat transfer. For heat pumps, their higher performance makes them the preferred auxiliary source, with electric resistance as backup. The prototype shows the feasibility of combining embedded control, web-based data, and user interaction to enhance technical and economic performance. The work provides a practical framework for energy-aware control in hybrid thermal systems, aiding cost reduction, renewable integration, and reduced environmental impact in buildings and hotels.

description: Thermoelectric cooling (TEC) modules are increasingly evaluated for compact thermal management, but their environmental performance strongly depends on the operating condition considered in life cycle assessment. These operating data were linked to ReCiPe midpoint indicators for production, transport, use-phase electricity and waste electric and electronic equipment treatment. The analysis focused on three ReCiPe midpoint indicators: global warming potential, fossil resource scarcity and mineral resource scarcity. The results indicate that the absolute environmental response is primarily determined by use-phase electricity demand. The lower impacts occurred in the higher efficiency region of the operating domain, whereas low efficiency conditions substantially increased cradle-to-grave burdens through higher use-phase electricity demand. Global warming potential and fossil resource scarcity were dominated by the use phase across the operating domain. Mineral resource scarcity followed a similar absolute trend but retained a stronger contribution related with the production. The main outcome is that the consideration of an operating point is a first-order parameter in thermoelectric cooling life cycle assessment, requiring explicit reporting and sensitivity analysis to avoid generalising environmental results from a single operating condition.

description: Nickel-phosphorus (Ni-P) coatings are widely employed due to their excellent hardness, wear resistance, corrosion performance, and optical properties. Since phosphorus content governs the transition from crystalline to amorphous structures, understanding its influence on functional properties is essential for designing tailored coatings. This work systematically investigates the effect of phosphorus incorporation on the composition, microstructure, morphology, optical response, and tribological behaviour of electrodeposited Ni-P coatings. Ni-P coatings were electrodeposited on 316L stainless steel using a citrate-based electrolyte containing 0-0.90 mol/L H₃PO₃. Deposition was performed at 50 °C and 25 mA/cm² for 20 min in a two-electrode configuration with a high-purity Ni anode. Coating composition and thickness were analysed by SEM/EDS, morphology and surface topography by SEM and AFM, crystalline structure by XRD, optical properties by spectrophotometry, and tribological performance by pin-on-disk testing under dry sliding conditions. Phosphorus incorporation increased non-linearly with H₃PO₃ concentration, revealing two distinct deposition regimes corresponding to crystalline low-P and amorphous high-P coatings. Increasing phosphorus levels promoted progressive grain refinement, resulting in denser, smoother surfaces with reduced roughness. XRD confirmed the structural evolution from crystalline FCC Ni to predominantly amorphous coatings through progressive peak broadening. These microstructural changes were directly reflected in functional properties. Higher phosphorus contents reduced reflectivity and brightness, resulting in darker matte coatings (L* ≈ 69), while simultaneously improving tribological performance by lowering and stabilizing the coefficient of friction (≈ 0.30). Variations in coating thickness were consistent with changes in deposition efficiency. The results demonstrate that phosphorus content is a key parameter for tailoring the structural and functional characteristics of electrodeposited Ni-P coatings. Establishing these correlations provides a practical framework for optimizing coatings for both engineering and decorative applications and supports future developments involving post-deposition treatments and multilayer architectures.

description:
In this study, sustainable bioactive composite films for bone tissue engineering  were developed based on chitosan, potato peel-derived cellulose, and hydroxyapatite (HAp) synthesized via a green sol–gel route using *Hylocereus undatus* cladode extract. By combining agro-industrial waste valorization with plant-mediated synthesis, the proposed materials embrace circular economy principles while addressing the need for environmentally responsible biomaterials. Chitosan provides biodegradability, cytocompatibility, and intrinsic antibacterial activity, whereas cellulose contributes mechanical reinforcement and structural stability. HAp enhances osteoconductivity, although its brittleness requires incorporation within a polymeric matrix.
In this context, cellulose was isolated using a mild, low-chemical extraction process and blended with chitosan, with the 80/20 (w/w) composition selected for its optimal balance of tensile strength (~62 MPa) and antibacterial performance. The matrix was subsequently reinforced with 0.10 and 0.15% (w/w) HAp nanoparticles. Structural, chemical, and surface characterization was performed using XRD, FTIR, Raman spectroscopy, SEM, EDS, AFM, and water contact angle measurements. Mechanical properties were evaluated by tensile testing and electrical behaviour by impedance spectroscopy. Bioactivity was investigated through immersion in simulated body fluid, and antibacterial performance was evaluated against *Staphylococcus aureus* and *Escherichia coli*. The composite containing 0.15% HAp (CC-H15) exhibited the highest tensile strength (~69 MPa), stable electrical behaviour at physiological temperature, effective antibacterial activity against both bacterial strains, and pronounced apatite-forming ability. Overall, these results demonstrate that the synergistic integration of waste-derived cellulose and green-synthesized HAp within a chitosan matrix yields a multifunctional, bioactive, and sustainable material with significant potential for next-generation bone-regenerative interfaces.

description:
Solar Heat for Industrial Processes (SHIP) systems utilising Linear Fresnel Collector (LFC) technology offer a promising approach to decarbonising industrial heat demand. The structure of the industrial load profile is a critical design variable that determines system sizing, storage requirements, and the Levelised Cost of Heat (LCOH). Despite this, the interplay between the temporal characteristics of demand and the variability of solar resources across different geographical locations has not been thoroughly investigated.
This study conducts a multi-location assessment of LFC-based SHIP systems integrated with thermal energy storage (TES) across eight sites: Portugal, Spain, Italy, Croatia, Turkey, Morocco, Tunisia, and Algeria. The system configuration includes a solar field, a TES unit, and a Steam Generator (SG) operating at 25 bar and up to 220 °C, delivering steam at 8 bar for medium-temperature industrial applications.
A parametric design framework, implemented in Python and integrated with Greenius software, is used to evaluate system performance across four industrial operating profiles (10/5, 10/7, 24/5, and 24/7, representing daily hours and weekly days). The analysis maintains a constant annual heat demand across all profiles. Various combinations of solar field size and TES capacity are examined to determine their effects on LCOH and Solar Fraction (SF). The solution spaces are assessed using the Empirical Lower Envelope Method (ELEM), which identifies the minimum achievable LCOH across successive SF intervals and provides a continuous representation of cost-optimal performance throughout the range of solar penetration.
The primary objective is to elucidate how local solar resources interact with industrial demand and to assess whether structural insights derived from a single location are transferable across the Mediterranean region. Preliminary simulations indicate that daily operating duration has a significant impact on LCOH and SF. This study aims to determine whether these effects are consistent across locations with differing solar resource conditions.

description:
Although Ti6Al4V is one of the most widely used titanium alloys for biomedical implants, implant-associated infections caused by bacterial adhesion continue to compromise its long-term clinical performance. In this study, magnesium oxide (MgO) nanoparticles were produced through an environmentally friendly synthesis route using Mangifera indica peel extract and employed as antibacterial coatings on Ti6Al4V substrates by electrophoretic deposition (EPD). Based on thermal analysis, the synthesized powders were calcined at 500 °C and 700 °C to investigate the influence of heat treatment on their structural and functional properties.
Phase identification by X-ray diffraction, supported by Rietveld refinement, confirmed the formation of crystalline cubic MgO with phase purities of 82.01 wt.% after calcination at 500 °C and 98.72 wt.% at 700 °C. Increasing the calcination temperature promoted crystal growth, yielding an average crystallite size of approximately 62 nm for the sample treated at 700 °C. Scanning electron microscopy further revealed a morphological evolution from strongly agglomerated particles to well-defined polyhedral structures.
The antibacterial performance of the MgO nanoparticles calcined at 700 °C was assessed against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus. Bacterial viability decreased as nanoparticle concentration increased, with significant inhibition observed from 3 mg/mL for E. coli and 6 mg/mL for S. aureus. This antimicrobial activity coincided with an increase in the culture medium pH, reaching values close to 10 at the highest nanoparticle concentrations. Uniform MgO coatings were successfully deposited on Ti6Al4V by EPD, and the coated substrates exhibited antibacterial activity, particularly against S. aureus. These findings demonstrate that integrating green-synthesized MgO nanoparticles with electrophoretic deposition offers a promising and sustainable strategy for producing antibacterial titanium surfaces for future biomedical applications.

description:
This article presents a set of case studies related to changes made to HVAC (heating, ventilation, and air conditioning) systems during building construction. It is during this phase that incompatibilities between specialties, structural limitations, omissions, and errors in the initial design—among other issues—are identified; when addressed in an integrated manner, these factors lead to solutions that improve the operation, efficiency, and reliability of building systems.
Several issues involving HVAC systems are presented, highlighting the need to adapt design solutions to the actual conditions on-site. In each case, the solution envisaged in the design, the problem identified on-site, and the technical analysis that supported the need for modification and the suggestion of a new solution are presented, while evaluating the technical, economic, and functional impacts of the choices made.
The selected case studies – indoor pressure control in critical sterilization areas, material selection and modifications in pressurized hydraulic and gas networks, improvement in the acoustic performance of indoor environments – reflect real-world examples, demonstrating that adapting solutions is an intrinsic part of the construction process and should not be interpreted solely as a consequence of limitations or constraints not identified during the design phase. In many situations, the changes implemented result from the need to coordinate between specialties, to address the technical conditions of the installation, to comply with regulatory requirements not fully defined, or to optimize costs and construction processes.
This article aims to demonstrate the importance of critically analyzing HVAC design and the resulting theoretical and practical rationale for the changes made, emphasizing the role of engineering in resolving complex situations and proposing solutions that ensure the functional and energy performance of a building and its sustainability.
title: HVAC Modifications: Case Studies and Engineering Solutions

description: This study experimentally investigated the effect of different roof covering materials on the energy generation performance of photovoltaic (PV) systems. For this purpose, two different roof configurations were constructed on the campus of the Faculty of Engineering at Trakya University. One of the roof systems was covered with trapezoidal steel panel, while the other was covered with shingles. Photovoltaic panels with identical technical specifications and a nominal power rating of 600W were installed on both roof systems. To ensure a reliable comparison of the experimental results, both PV panels were installed facing south, and the roof inclination angle was maintained at a constant value of 25° for both systems. In addition, environmental parameters that could influence system performance were continuously monitored throughout the experimental period. Meteorological variables, including solar irradiance and ambient temperature, were periodically measured and incorporated into the performance evaluation. The voltage and current values of the photovoltaic panels were continuously recorded at 5-minute intervals over a 31-day period from 01.07.2025 to 31.07.2025. Based on the measured data, the instantaneous power output and total energy generation were calculated, and the performance of the two roof systems was comparatively evaluated. The experimental results showed that the PV panel installed on the shingle-covered roof generated a total of 95.6kWh, whereas the PV panel mounted on the trapezoidal steel roof produced 90.5kWh of electrical energy. These findings demonstrate that the shingle-covered roof provided superior energy generation performance. The primary reason for this performance difference is that the shingle roof exhibited a lower surface temperature than the trapezoidal steel roof. The reduced roof surface temperature consequently lowered the operating temperature of the photovoltaic panel, thereby improving its energy conversion efficiency. It was determined that a lower PV operating temperature has a positive effect on the energy generation performance of photovoltaic systems.
title: Comparative Analysis of the Effect of Roof Covering Types on Energy Production in Photovoltaic Systems

description: In this study, the convective drying kinetics and transient moisture dynamics of wool yarn bobbins—a high-cost and time-consuming process in the textile industry—were modeled using an Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS). Drying experiments were conducted on bobbins consisting of a 65% wool and 35% Orlon blend under an air flow rate of 450 m³h-1, a temperature of 100 °C, and a gauge pressure of 2 bar. Throughout the process, temperature variations were monitored in radial directions via thermocouples embedded within the yarn bobbin. The initially established standard ANFIS models produced unstable results, yielding a negative coefficient of determination (R2) and high root mean square error (RMSE) values due to thermal lag effects within the system and rule explosion associated with the curse of dimensionality. To overcome these limitations, data leakage was prevented by chronologically splitting the time-series dataset into an 80% training/validation block and a 20% testing block. Through feature importance analysis, the input space was reduced to the most critical variables, and autoregressive time-lagged parameters from the previous time steps (t-1,(t-2) and (t-3) were incorporated into the model. Furthermore, to prevent local oscillations during gradient descent steps in the optimization phase, the Takagi-Sugeno type ANFIS architecture was optimized using a dynamic learning rate damping mechanism. The finalized model demonstrated an outstanding prediction performance on the independent test dataset. In predicting the mass loss value, the model achieved an R2 of 0.9052, an RMSE of 0.0312, MAE of 0.0253; and a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 0.52%. Consequently, the proposed optimized methodology completely eliminated the matrix instabilities encountered in the initial designs, providing a stable, reliable, and highly accurate soft computing alternative for real-time moisture monitoring and intelligent control mechanisms in industrial textile drying operations.
title: Computing Approach for Real-Time Mass Loss Prediction in Industrial Wool Bobbin Dehydration Processes

description:
An industrial urea-recovery effluent supplies a fixed ammonia and water vapor stream. This work examines whether that stream, burned with air supplied stoichiometrically for the incoming ammonia, can sustain stable flames while keeping NO emissions below typical compliance limits, or whether supplemental methane or hydrogen is required.

A one-dimensional free-flame solver in Cantera is coupled with constant-pressure homogeneous reactors to calculate ignition delay and peak heat-release rate. Both simulations use the CRECK_upHCNtS detailed mechanism. The parameter sweep covers inlet temperatures from 873 to 1600 K, water vapor mole fractions from 0.30 to 0.55, and target equivalence ratios from 0.5 to 1.5.

No point in the investigated envelope required supplemental fuel. Every flame reached a maximum temperature above 1550 K and ignited in less than 0.5 s. Adding ten percentage points of water vapor to the base stream reduced outlet NO by about 20 percent. Increasing the target equivalence ratio from 0.70 to 1.20 reduced NO by approximately a factor of two. At a target equivalence ratio of 1.50, NO remained below 1000 ppm for inlet temperatures up to 1417 K.

When supplemental fuel is injected, the workflow also reports carbon intensity and NO emissions per unit of delivered energy. This allows the decarbonization penalty of any pilot-fuel strategy to be evaluated directly.
title: Supplemental-Fuel-Free Stabilization of Ammonia–Water Industrial Effluent Flames with Low NO Emissions

description:
Accurate prediction of turbulent flow fields remains a significant challenge in Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD), particularly when high-fidelity simulations are computationally expensive. Data-driven surrogate models provide an attractive alternative but often fail to preserve the governing physical laws, resulting in physically inconsistent predictions. This work presents a hybrid machine learning framework for physics-guided correction of Reynolds-Averaged Navier–Stokes (RANS) solutions for the classical two-dimensional Backward-Facing Step (BFS) benchmark.

The proposed methodology learns correction mappings between coarse- and fine-mesh CFD solutions generated with OpenFOAM. A Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) is first employed as a purely data-driven baseline to estimate velocity and pressure corrections. Subsequently, a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) introduces physics-based regularisation by enforcing the continuity equation and, in ongoing developments, the steady momentum equations. Rather than replacing the CFD solver, the proposed framework acts as a physics-guided corrector that aims to improve numerical predictions while enforcing physical consistency.

Model performance is evaluated using Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), Relative Error Reduction (RER), and residual-based physical consistency metrics. Preliminary experiments indicate that data-driven models effectively reduce interpolation errors between CFD meshes, whereas physics-informed constraints improve physical consistency while revealing the trade-off between predictive accuracy and conservation-law enforcement. These findings provide valuable insights into the development of hybrid surrogate models for turbulent flow reconstruction.

Furthermore, the proposed methodology supports computationally efficient CFD workflows by combining data-driven learning with embedded physical constraints, enabling more reliable surrogate models for engineering flow prediction.

The present study provides a foundation for future research involving turbulence-aware residuals, adaptive loss weighting, additional turbulence closure information, and validation using higher-fidelity benchmark CFD datasets.

description:
In-situ adaptive tabulation (ISAT), introduced by Pope in 1997 for turbulent combustion chemistry, is adapted here to accelerate the thermodynamic map that governs multicomponent droplet evaporation and condensation in Lagrangian particle tracking.

The map is a coupled vapor-liquid equilibrium calculation using the UNIFAC activity model, a Rachford-Rice flash, and the Full Differential Diffusion mass-transfer solver of Sacomano et al. It differs from the Arrhenius-based rate map used in classical ISAT in three main ways.

First, the natural first component of the state vector, with dimension 5 + 3Ncomp, is a geometric length scale rather than temperature. This invalidates the combustion-specific realizability check. Second, the output vector, with dimension 2 + 2Ncomp, includes the per-species mass transfer rates, the latent heats, and the two convective coupling scalars hconvA and Slat. This favors rates mode, referred to as Option C, over delta-state mode, referred to as Option D. Third, the implementation requires two-site wiring into the NL-CVODES BDF integrator, so that the physical oracle is intercepted only after a successful retrieval.

We also document a side effect of deterministic tabulation that, to our knowledge, has not been reported in the ISAT literature. The cache eliminates the order 10^-6 numerical noise of the iterative Sacomano solver. As a result, BDF Newton iterations are reduced from 8–16 to 2, and the BDF success rate increases from 40–100 percent to 100 percent.

In a production industrial spray case with seven condensable species, the table saturates at 450 leaves after approximately 5 × 10^5 queries, with a steady-state retrieval rate of 100 percent and no physical regression. Combined with an analytical per-component Jacobian and a frozen film-property cache, the full optimization stack reduces CVODES cost by 68 percent and total wall-clock time by 40 percent.
title: Accelerating VLE-Based Spray Evaporation Models with In-Situ Adaptive Tabulation

description:
The predictive monitoring of rotating machinery is vital for ensuring reliability and operational safety in critical industrial systems. However, the early identification of anomalies imposes complex technological challenges. Unlike the isolated analysis of components, rotating assemblies exhibit coupled structural dynamics that result in highly non-linear and multivariate global vibration signatures. These are frequently masked by process noise and severe operational fluctuations, further compounded by a chronic scarcity of labelled historical failure data.
To address this, this study proposes an unsupervised, data-driven approach for detecting incipient degradation by integrating the Kernel Cumulative Sum (K-CUSUM) algorithm with a statistical validation mechanism based on the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) unit root test. In contrast to classical parametric methods requiring restrictive data distribution assumptions or intricate physical models, the proposed methodology maps the complex vibratory signals into a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). Within this higher-dimensional space, the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) metric is evaluated sequentially via an iterated kernel function, providing robustness in quantifying persistent stochastic deviations from the healthy reference distribution.
To mitigate false alarms arising from legitimate operational transitions, such as abrupt load and speed variations, the ADF test acts as a dynamic regime validator. It enables the autonomous updating of the monitoring baseline exclusively when the statistical stationarity of the new operational profile is proven. The synergy of these techniques culminates in a highly adaptive detection system, capable of isolating process variations and tracking embryonic structural anomalies. Results demonstrate the methodology's efficacy in extracting degradation indicators with high precision. Ultimately, this approach provides scalable and computationally efficient architecture for predictive monitoring, playing a decisive role in mitigating catastrophic failures, reducing unscheduled downtimes, and maximising the useful life cycle of rotating machinery.
title: Predictive monitoring; Rotating Machinery; Anomaly detection; K-CUSUM; RKHS

description:
Helical strakes are used to suppress vortex-induced vibrations in subsea risers, but high-fidelity fluid-structure interaction simulations are too computationally expensive for systematic geometric design.

In this work, a linear regression surrogate is constructed to relate three vane parameters, namely height, length, and helix angle, to the root-mean-square lift coefficient, CL,RMS, on a riser with diameter D = 0.325 m, Reynolds number Re = 1.81 × 10^5, and reduced velocity u* = 5.

A central composite design with fifteen coupled CFD/FEM simulations using the MFSim platform provides the training set. An additional fifteen geometries sampled from a normal distribution are used as an independent test set.

Correlation analysis shows that helix angle has negligible influence on CL,RMS, allowing the surrogate to be reduced to two predictors. The resulting two-variable linear model achieves a mean absolute percentage error of 6.32 percent and an R² value of 0.82 on the test set.

Vane height is the dominant parameter. CL,RMS decreases monotonically with both vane height and vane length, which is consistent with the breakdown of spanwise-coherent vortex structures into smaller, lower-energy eddies as vane blockage increases.

At a fixed length near the design center, increasing vane height from 54 mm to 87 mm reduces CL,RMS by 52 percent. This demonstrates the usefulness of the surrogate for rapid preliminary design screening.
title: Linear Surrogate Modeling of Helical Strake Geometry for VIV Reduction in Subsea Risers

description:
The increasing integration of renewable energy sources, storage systems, and distributed energy resources has made the operation of microgrids more complex. In this context, power electronics converters play an important role, as they enable the connection between different sources, loads, and the electrical grid. They also control variables such as voltage, current, active power, and reactive power.
The high penetration of inverter-based resources introduces new technical challenges, namely operation in weak grids, reduced inertia, the variability of renewable generation, rapid load changes, and the need to maintain voltage and frequency stability.
This work analyses the potential of Artificial Intelligence applied to the control and operation of power converters in microgrids, with particular focus on grid-following and grid-forming inverters. At a later stage, the model is also associated with an artificial intelligence technique applied to inverter control, allowing its effect on the dynamic behaviour of the system to be evaluated. The objective is to compare the conventional control strategy with an Artificial Intelligence-assisted approach, enabling the analysis of important system parameters. The simulation component provides a basis for understanding the performance of the inverter and assessing the potential of intelligent techniques in the development of control strategies for microgrid applications.

description: The growing demand for condition monitoring strategies has driven the development of techniques capable of estimating dynamic variables without requiring direct instrumentation at every point of interest. In rotating machinery, limitations associated with sensor placement, instrumentation costs, and harsh operating conditions prevent the acquisition of complete information about the vibratory behavior of the system, making virtual sensing a promising alternative for reconstructing responses that cannot be directly measured. In this context, this study investigates the application of the Kalman Filter algorithm to the virtual sensing of rotating machinery with the objective of enhancing monitoring capabilities in rotordynamic systems. A finite element model of a flexible rotor was developed using the ROSS library to represent the dynamic behavior of the system. The Kalman Filter algorithm was then employed to estimate the rotor dynamic responses from a reduced set of vibration measurements, enabling the reconstruction of responses at non-instrumented locations. Furthermore, the filter covariance matrices were tuned through a multi-objective optimization procedure based on the Differential Evolution Method combined with a compromise programming approach to improve the estimation accuracy. The proposed methodology was evaluated by comparing the estimated responses with numerical reference data obtained from the finite element model. The results showed excellent agreement between the predicted and reference responses, demonstrating the capability of the proposed approach to accurately reconstruct vibration amplitudes at uninstrumented locations while maintaining low estimation errors. The optimized covariance matrices significantly improved the estimation performance by providing an appropriate balance between model and measurement uncertainties. Overall, the integration of rotordynamic modeling, the KF, and the DE-Method proved to be an effective and robust framework for virtual sensing in rotating machinery. The proposed methodology represents a promising alternative for expanding monitoring coverage while reducing instrumentation requirements, thereby supporting more reliable condition monitoring and predictive maintenance strategies for rotating systems.

description: Primary atomisation generates a broad range of liquid structures whose downstream dispersion is prohibitively expensive to resolve with interface-capturing methods. Hybrid Euler–Lagrange strategies address this by converting resolved Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) structures into Lagrangian droplets (Discrete Particle Model, DPM); however, the conversion must be physically representative and strictly conservative. This work presents and validates such a conversion framework implemented in the multiphase solver MFSim. Three methodologies of increasing fidelity are compared. The simplest assigns a single droplet per structure. The second introduces a morphological classification: a per-structure eccentricity and aspect ratio label each connected structure as droplet, ligament, or Eulerian (vetoed), and ligaments are converted as geometric strings of droplets. The most complete adds the physical fragmentation of ligaments through a segmented linear-stability analysis, in which the Weber number drives a dispersion relation whose most unstable wavenumber sets the ligament and droplet diameters, and therefore the number of generated parcels. The framework is fully integrated with block-structured adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) and MPI domain decomposition. Structures that span refinement levels or process boundaries are handled by a two-pass cross-boundary exchange that reconstructs global metrics, relative velocities, and centrelines. Mass, momentum, and energy are conserved in every conversion, with dedicated treatment of droplet thermal energy. An extensive verification campaign covers the methodologies under a wide range of conditions, including different refinement-level differences, serial and parallel (MPI) decompositions, statically and dynamically refined meshes, the available overlap-control strategies, and both uniform and sheared velocity fields. In every case the parallel results reproduce the serial ones and the conserved quantities are preserved, providing a robust, decomposition-invariant basis for predictive spray simulations.
title: A conservative Euler–Lagrange conversion framework for primary atomisation: morphological classification and linear-stability fragmentation on adaptive parallel meshes

description: Robotic sealant deposition is widely used in industrial applications requiring high geometric accuracy and repeatability, such as in the automotive, aerospace, and advanced manufacturing sectors. Among the factors affecting bead quality, the orientation of the end-effector relative to the trajectory plays a fundamental role, particularly when curved paths are employed. This work experimentally investigates the influence of Tool Center Point (TCP) rotation during the robotic deposition of polyurethane sealant (PU40) along a circular arc trajectory. The experiments were carried out using a Hanwha HCR-14 collaborative robot equipped with a Makita DCG180 caulking gun. Two deposition strategies were compared: (i) arc motion without TCP rotation, maintaining constant tool orientation throughout the trajectory, and (ii) arc motion with TCP rotation, maintaining the tool tangent to the trajectory. Due to limitations of the robot controller, the deposition speed was adjusted when using TCP rotation to ensure equivalent conditions between the experiments. The beads were characterised by laser profilometry using a Keyence LJ-X8060 profilometer to acquire data before and after curing, allowing the evaluation of geometric changes and dimensional stability. The results showed that deposition without TCP rotation promoted bead twisting, characterised by the displacement of the material outlet across the cross-section during deposition. In contrast, TCP rotation significantly reduced this effect; however, the robotic manipulator exhibited limitations in performing this motion, introducing geometric oscillations in the beads as well as inaccuracies in the programmed linear speed. The results demonstrate that TCP orientation directly influences the quality of robotic sealant deposition, highlighting the trade-off between bead geometric fidelity and the kinematic stability of the robotic manipulator along curved trajectories, making it an important parameter to control in industrial processes.

description:
Accurate modelling of continuous mechanical dynamical systems is fundamental to computational engineering, where ordinary differential equations (ODEs) describe the evolution of structural and vibrational phenomena. Classical numerical integration methods provide reliable approximations but require explicit mathematical models and suitable solver selection. Neural Ordinary Differential Equations (Neural ODEs) have recently emerged as an alternative machine learning framework capable of learning continuous system dynamics directly from observational data, offering new possibilities for computational modelling and reduced-order representations.

This work presents a comparative assessment of Neural ODEs and classical numerical integration methods for modelling mechanical dynamical systems. A mass–spring oscillator is adopted as the benchmark problem because of its relevance in vibration analysis and computational mechanics. The evaluated numerical methods include the Forward Euler, Heun, fourth-order Runge–Kutta (RK4), and adaptive ODE solvers. Neural ODEs are trained to reconstruct the continuous system dynamics directly from trajectory data, enabling a direct comparison with conventional integration techniques.

Model performance is evaluated in terms of Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), trajectory reconstruction accuracy, interpolation capability, extrapolation behaviour, and computational cost. The experimental analysis highlights the strengths and limitations of Neural ODEs relative to traditional numerical solvers, discussing the trade-offs between predictive accuracy, generalisation capability, and computational efficiency in continuous-time dynamical system modelling.

Furthermore, the proposed comparative framework offers a systematic basis for evaluating continuous-time learning approaches in engineering applications, supporting the development of robust computational models for simulation, prediction, and reduced-order system representation.

The results contribute to the understanding of data-driven approaches for mechanical system simulation and provide a foundation for future investigations involving scientific machine learning, physics-informed learning, reduced-order modelling, and digital twin applications in computational engineering.

description: The balancing of rotating machines is an essential procedure for the reduction of vibrations and bearing loads. The results demonstrated that the AKF, combined with the optimization of the uncertainty covariance matrices, was able to estimate the unbalance forces at the rotor disks with high accuracy, using only the "measured" vibratory responses and the mathematical model. It is concluded that the AKF-based approach constitutes a robust and viable tool for online application, allowing the effective balancing of rotating machines without the need for downtime to insert trial weights or a perfectly calibrated finite element model.

description:
In recent years, machine learning techniques have been increasingly applied to automatic fault identification and condition monitoring systems. Among these approaches, anomaly detection methods are commonly used to evaluate signals acquired under nominal operating conditions, with deviations from established monitoring patterns interpreted as potential indicators of faults. However, some systems present complex dynamic behavior, in which a fault-related anomaly may appear either as a pronounced variation or as a subtle signal modification, depending on the physical source disturbing the system.
This study investigates the use of acoustic signals and machine learning methods for fault detection, using a hair dryer as an experimental case study. The hair dryer was selected because it naturally generates broadband noise associated with airflow and heating, while also containing a high-speed rotary motor operating at approximately 20,000 rpm with speed control. The system was physically modified to introduce different fault-like conditions, including minor perturbations caused by partial airflow blockage and more pronounced changes produced by imbalance in one of the rotor blades. An audio acquisition setup was assembled to ensure experimental repeatability. A total of 40 samples were acquired at two different speeds for each operating condition: normal operation, obstructed airflow, and rotor imbalance. This resulted in six operating classes and 240 audio samples.
The proposed signal processing methodology involved: bandpass filtering using a fourth-order Butterworth filter in the 5–10 kHz frequency range; noise reduction using the Discrete Wavelet Transform with a Symlet 4 wavelet and three decomposition levels; and feature extraction based on RMS, mean spectral centroid, mean spectral flatness, and Mel Frequency Cepstral Coefficients. The extracted features were then used to train and compare classification models through a machine learning benchmarking framework. The best-performing model was a decision tree classifier, which achieved highly accurate classification performance in distinguishing the imposed operating conditions.

description: High-fidelity Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations resolving all relevant spatio-temporal scales remain computationally prohibitive for large-scale, many-query scenarios such as aerospace design optimisation. Alternatively, low-fidelity simulations on coarse grids offer significant computational savings, but suffer from substantial discretisation errors that severely compromise predictive accuracy and reliability. This work presents a data-driven, machine learning framework that acts as a surrogate corrector, trained to predict and eliminate these inherent errors without requiring the overhead of full spatio-temporal refinement. Unlike traditional empirical corrections, high-fidelity data is projected onto coarse meshes, allowing supervised learning algorithms to model the complex, non-linear relationship between local coarse-grid flow features and the corresponding local discretisation error. Several ML architectures are systematically evaluated and compared, including Random Forests, Neural Networks, and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In particular, geometric deep learning, via GNNs, is deployed to exploit neighbourhood aggregation and respect grid topology on unstructured meshes, yielding smooth predictions and superior generalisation near flow discontinuities such as shock waves, where simpler regressors tend to struggle. Operating either as a post-processing enhancement or iteratively within a solver-in-the-loop framework for unsteady flows, the methodology is rigorously validated across a diverse range of steady and unsteady compressible aerodynamic test cases. Results demonstrate that while Random Forests provide a robust and computationally cheap baseline, GNNs consistently deliver the highest predictive fidelity on unstructured meshes, generalising well across varying flow conditions. Ultimately, this machine learning-augmented approach drastically reduces wall-clock cost whilst recovering near high-fidelity accuracy across diverse flow regimes. The integration of geometric deep learning directly into numerical solvers paves the way for highly efficient aerodynamic design processes and the viable deployment of aerospace digital twins without sacrificing physical realism.

description:
ACM Framework™
An Integrated Methodology for Asset Criticality Assessment and Strategic Maintenance Decision-Making

Asset criticality assessment is a fundamental element in maintenance planning, risk management, and strategic asset management. Although indicators such as Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF), Mean Time to Repair (MTTR), and preventive maintenance plans are widely used in industry, they are often applied independently and do not always provide sufficient support for strategic maintenance decision-making.

This paper proposes the ACM Framework™ (Asset Criticality Mapping), a structured methodology developed from practical industrial experience to support maintenance prioritization through the integration of operational criticality, maintenance performance, and risk assessment. The framework originated from the observation that assets with significantly different impacts on production, safety, quality, and operational continuity are frequently managed using similar maintenance strategies, resulting in inefficient resource allocation and limited decision support.

The proposed methodology integrates multiple operational criteria, including production impact, safety, quality, environmental impact, maintenance cost, reliability indicators (MTBF and MTTR), and spare parts lead time into a weighted criticality model (ACM Score™). Based on the calculated score, the framework supports asset classification, maintenance strategy definition, operational risk assessment, spare parts management, and integration with Maintenance Planning and Control (MPC/PCM), following the principles of ISO 55000 for asset management.

Unlike traditional approaches that primarily evaluate equipment performance through isolated maintenance indicators, the ACM Framework™ provides a structured decision-support model focused on the operational consequences of asset failures and their strategic importance within industrial systems.

The methodology is currently in its final development stage, and future work will focus on its experimental validation through industrial case studies to assess its applicability, robustness, and contribution to maintenance decision-making and strategic asset management.

Aiming for financial optimization, an architecture was developed that eliminates the traditional differential, replacing it with independent transfer cases that house these gear pairs. Segregated lubrication was also implemented for the reducer and cases, facilitating maintenance and the set's tribological efficiency.

The sizing of shafts, keys and gears relied on established analytical methodologies for machine design, with data subsequently validated through the MITCalc software. Based on this, computational modeling (CAD) was elaborated, and Finite Element Analysis (FEA) was applied to evaluate the static stresses within housings and transmission elements, estimating their fatigue resistance. Furthermore, specific bearings were selected to withstand operational loads, stipulating an approximate useful life of two full competitive years.

The results attested the system’s technical viability, exhibiting adequate safety factors and an estimated longevity of three competitive cycles. The proposed arrangement combined structural safety with simplicity in machining, heat treatments, and assembly, consolidating itself as a low-cost alternative to solutions from the same category.

In summary, the developed 4x4 system proved itself feasible, robust, and financially viable. The study gave the mechanical engineering undergraduates valuable experience, transforming theory into real skills for the current job market.

description: The thermal performance of solar air heater (SAH) is usually hindered due to low convective heat transfer coefficient between the absorber plate and flowing air. Passive heat transfer enhancement techniques such as vortex generators and twisted tape inserts are popular promising solutions to increase the thermal performance with less energy supplied from external sources. In this study, an experimental study is conducted to investigate and compare the thermohydraulic performance of a solar air heater with three new hybrid tape configurations to produce different flow structures and vortex intensities. The effect of each hybrid tape was investigated by experiments through the same operating conditions during a typical range of Reynolds numbers on the heat transfer and hydraulic characteristics. The performance of the three configurations was analyzed in terms of outlet air temperature, thermal efficiency, Nusselt number, friction factor, pressure drop and thermo-hydraulic performance parameter (THPP) and compared with that of a conventional smooth duct solar air heater . The results show that all the three hybrid tape configurations significantly improve the convective heat transfer by enhanced flow mixing and thermal boundary layer disruption. But the hydraulic penalties are different because of the different vortex strength and flow resistance. Among the studied configurations, Hybrid Tape-II has the best thermo-hydraulic performance, giving the best compromise between heat transfer enhancement and pressure loss. Hence, it is the most suitable configuration for solar air heater applications. The results indicate that the properly designed hybrid tape inserts are a simple, low cost, and energy efficient passive technique to enhance the performance of renewable thermal systems and provide practical guidelines for the design of high-efficiency solar air heaters.
title: Experimental Thermohydraulic Performance Analysis of a Solar Air Heater Incorporating Hybrid Vortex Generators for Sustainable Thermal Energy Applications

description:
Linear Ramping is a tool entry strategy used in milling operations, particularly when it is not possible to initiate the cut outside the workpiece material. Compared with vertical tool entry (plunge milling), ramp milling imposes lower mechanical loads on the cutting tool, thereby reducing the risk of vibrations and tool wear while promoting more efficient chip evacuation [1, 2].
In industrial practice, ramp milling is widely employed in roughing operations performed on CNC machining centres and is frequently incorporated into CAM strategies to increase productivity and extend tool life. Given the importance of the ramp milling strategy and considering that its performance depends on several parameters, including the ramp angle, feed rate, cutting speed, tool diameter, and workpiece material properties, it was considered relevant to conduct an experimental study on this topic.
This research was carried out in collaboration with the Portuguese cutting tool manufacturer Palbit, which supplied the milling tools used to machine the EN AW-7075 aluminium alloy. The company also contributed to the initial definition of the cutting conditions and machining parameters adopted in the experimental investigation.
An 8 mm diameter endmill was used throughout the study. The process was characterised by performing ramp milling operations with ramp angles of 1°, 2°, and 3°, until reaching a depth equal to the tool diameter. The investigation focused on evaluating tool wear, the surface roughness of the machined channels, and the vibration levels recorded during the milling process. The results obtained provided important insights into the advantages and limitations of the ramp milling strategy.

description:
Diabetes Mellitus is one of the most significant global public health challenges, with diabetic foot representing one of its most severe complications. Early detection of plantar thermal abnormalities may help prevent ulcers, as localized temperature increases can precede visible tissue damage. Additionally, the ability to monitor the evolution of existing wounds through thermal assessment is crucial for effective clinical management. Infrared thermography has emerged as a non-invasive technique capable of detecting such changes and supporting clinical screening and follow-up procedures.

This study presents the development and preliminary validation of a MATLAB-based application for the computational analysis of plantar thermograms. The application enables loading thermographic images and radiometric temperature matrices, selecting metatarsal Regions of Interest (ROIs), calculating thermal parameters, and assessing bilateral thermal asymmetries using mean and focal temperature differences between symmetrical plantar regions.

As direct access to a diabetic population was not available during the initial development phase, a thermal provocation protocol was conducted with healthy adult volunteers. A controlled thermal stimulus was applied to the metatarsal region with a previously heated coin, and the thermal recovery process was monitored for 7 minutes with a HIKMICRO M31 infrared camera. The thermograms were analyzed using the developed application and compared with results obtained with the HIKMICRO Analyzer software.

The application successfully identified and quantified induced focal thermal variations and allowed the monitoring of thermal recovery patterns over time. The comparison with the reference software demonstrated good agreement in the calculated thermal parameters, with occasional discrepancies attributed to experimental variability and challenges in bilateral anatomical correspondence.

These findings demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed computational approach and suggest that the developed application may serve as a useful tool for plantar thermal screening and early monitoring of the diabetic foot, supporting future studies involving diabetic patients.

description: Accurate and computationally efficient modeling of one-dimensional methane flames is essential for analyzing, designing, and optimizing combustion systems, particularly in engineering applications requiring repeated simulations of chemically reacting flows. Detailed kinetic mechanisms, such as GRI-Mech 3.0, are widely used to provide a comprehensive representation of methane oxidation through a large set of chemical species and elementary reactions; however, this level of detail substantially increases computational cost. Reduced kinetic mechanisms have therefore been developed to preserve the dominant reaction pathways while eliminating secondary species and reactions with limited influence on the main flame characteristics. This study compared detailed GRI-Mech 3.0 with a reduced mechanism based on Pope’s reduction principles for simulating a freely propagating, one-dimensional premixed methane flame. Both mechanisms were implemented in Python using the Cantera chemical-kinetics library and evaluated under equivalent numerical and operating conditions to ensure consistent comparison. The analysis considered computational processing time, spatial temperature profiles, adiabatic flame temperature, flame propagation characteristics, and mole-fraction distributions of principal reactants, products, and intermediate species. The predictive performance of the reduced mechanism was assessed by comparing deviations in the thermal and chemical profiles relative to the GRI-Mech 3.0 reference model, while computational efficiency was evaluated from the reduction in simulation time and chemical-model complexity. The reduced mechanism decreased simulation time by approximately 60% while preserving general temperature evolution, the principal flame characteristics, and the spatial behavior of the dominant chemical species with deviations under 5% within the evaluated conditions. Although localized differences were observed for some intermediate species, the overall thermal and chemical predictions maintained an error margin below 3% relative to detailed kinetics. These findings demonstrate that the reduced mechanism provides a suitable compromise between computational efficiency and predictive accuracy, supporting its application in more complex combustion simulations where the computational cost of detailed chemistry represents a significant limitation.

description: Green hydrogen is expected to play an important role in the decarbonisation of energy-intensive sectors and in the integration of variable renewable energy sources. However, its economic competitiveness is strongly influenced by electrolyser utilisation, electricity procurement costs and storage requirements. This study presents a techno-economic assessment of green hydrogen production using a 10 MW proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyser under operational and market assumptions representative of the Portuguese energy system. The Levelized Cost of Hydrogen (LCOH) calculator developed by the Portuguese National Laboratory of Energy and Geology (LNEG) was used to evaluate a reference case and three sensitivity scenarios concerning the electrolyser load factor, electricity price and compressed-hydrogen storage capacity. For a 60% load factor and an electricity price of 40 €/MWh, the estimated LCOH was 4.77 €/kg H₂. Increasing the load factor from 10% to 99% reduced the LCOH from 16.87 to 3.79 €/kg H₂, demonstrating the importance of electrolyser utilisation in recovering fixed investment costs. At a constant 60% load factor, electricity prices ranging from −5 to 250 €/MWh resulted in LCOH values between 2.20 and 16.73 €/kg H₂, confirming electricity procurement as the dominant economic driver. Under the adopted cost assumptions, incorporating compressed-hydrogen storage equivalent to 4–8 days of production increased the LCOH by only 0.11–0.22 €/kg H₂. The results highlight the importance of combining high electrolyser utilisation with stable, low-cost electricity procurement. They also suggest that appropriately sized storage may improve supply flexibility with a relatively limited impact on hydrogen production costs.

description:
Balise-based train control systems, such as CONVEL, are trackside signalling protocols used on the Portuguese railway network that derive from the ATC-2/EBICAB family. These systems, rely on trackside beacons ("balises") that transmit telegrams to onboard train equipment via short-range electromagnetic coupling. In these types of protocols, the trackside beacons, send fixed length telegrams when activated by a passing train. The messages are configurable, but present different fields for data, synchronisation and Hamming code protection bits.  The Hamming code protection bits and the fixed synchronisation words perform critical data integrity, timing, and alignment functions to ensure that the beacons transmit vital safety information to the train without errors or delays. Within this context, testing the infrastructure is a critical part of secure and reliable train circulation. 
The currently available testing infrastructure allows only a part of the data telegram payload to be varied, making it impossible to emulate communications flaws derived from Hamming code protection or synchronisation bit errors. Existing methods cannot validate the onboard train reception chain end-to-end. This motivates the need for a complete telegram generation and transmission through the real air-gap interface, as a real beacon would produce it.
To meet this need, a Hardware-in-The-Loop CONVEL Balise Simulator has been implemented that reproduces the complete generation and transmission of a beacon/balise telegram. The aim of the developed tool is to freely program every transmitted bit, thus allowing the injection of faults into the system. 
This paper describes the architecture and implementation of a laboratory equipment that emulates a real passive CONVEL Balise, based on a Complex Programmable Logic Device (CPLD) as well as the power electronics circuitry that receives and sends data to the train. 
This work is currently underway at Critical Software's railway test laboratory to emulate and detect both operating and faulty beacon/balise telegrams.

description: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations executed on high-performance computing (HPC) clusters generate extensive semi-structured logs containing residual histories, Courant-number information, iteration times, parallel-processing messages and solver failures. These records are essential for identifying numerical divergence, residual stagnation and execution faults, but their manual interpretation is time-consuming and strongly dependent on specialist knowledge. This paper presents the design and initial implementation of an on-premise middleware that combines deterministic log parsing with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for traceable analysis of CFD simulations. The pipeline ingests MFsim outputs and common engineering log formats, applies regular expressions and format validation to extract numerical indicators, and cross-checks the extracted values against reference calculations. The validated metrics and textual events are linked to a curated vector knowledge base containing solver documentation, technical manuals and troubleshooting records. A quantised local large language model uses retrieved evidence to explain detected events and formulate recommendations, whereas all numerical operations remain assigned to deterministic modules. The middleware operates as a parallel service in the HPC environment and accesses simulation records through workflows compatible with Slurm or PBS schedulers. Its assessment framework considers extraction accuracy, retrieval context precision and recall, response faithfulness, latency, processor and graphics-processing-unit usage, and the computational costs of indexing and inference. The implemented prototype establishes a reproducible path from raw CFD logs to evidence-linked diagnostic reports while retaining sensitive simulation data within local infrastructure. It also separates physical and numerical indicators from natural-language synthesis, improving auditability and reducing dependence on informal troubleshooting practices. The proposed architecture therefore provides a technically consistent foundation for decision support in computational fluid mechanics, particularly in laboratories requiring data sovereignty, interoperability with existing solvers and verifiable engineering recommendations.

description: This paper presents a machine learning pipeline for predicting aerodynamic coefficients of arbitrary airfoil geometries under subsonic flight conditions. This dissertation addresses the application of advanced modeling and machine learning techniques for monitoring and optimizing the reverse flotation process of iron ore, a critical step for removing impurities—particularly silica—that compromise the quality of the mineral concentrate. Supervised models, with emphasis on the XGBoost algorithm, were developed to predict the silica content in the final concentrate, while unsupervised methods, such as Isolation Forest and PCA, were applied to detect operational anomalies.

Results indicated that the iron content in the concentrate and the pulp level in Flotation Column 07 were the most relevant predictive variables, whereas fluctuations in air flow and pulp pH proved to be decisive for anomaly occurrences. These findings highlight the importance of combining continuous process monitoring with state-of-the-art data-driven approaches.

From an applied perspective, the proposed methodology demonstrates the potential of digital mining by providing real-time decision support, reducing dependence on time-consuming laboratory analyses, and contributing to process stability and efficiency. Beyond academic contributions, the study also evidences practical benefits in terms of sustainability, operational reliability, and final product quality. Furthermore, the proposed framework provides a foundation for future research involving hybrid predictive models, digital twins, and intelligent process control systems. The integration of data analytics with industrial operations reinforces the role of artificial intelligence in improving mineral processing performance, supporting safer, more efficient, and economically sustainable mining practices while enabling proactive operational decision-making in complex industrial environments.
