description: Multizone combustion models have been widely used as reduced-order tools for premixed and partially premixed flames, where the initial mixture composition is comparatively well defined. Diffusion flames, however, are governed by the local interaction between fuel transport, oxidiser entrainment, heat release and thermal stratification. This coupling makes their representation more demanding, especially when the objective is to retain physical interpretability without the computational cost of full computational fluid dynamics. This work investigates the application of a multizone thermofluid model to diffusion-controlled combustion. The domain is represented by interacting zones with distinct thermodynamic and composition states, while inter-zone exchange terms describe the transport processes responsible for mixture formation, energy redistribution and the development of reactive regions. The study focuses on the evolution of temperature, species stratification and heat-release behaviour under non-premixed conditions. Particular attention is given to the role of mass and energy exchange between zones, since these mechanisms control the transition from initially separated fuel and oxidiser streams towards mixed and burned products. The proposed formulation is assessed through representative diffusion-flame simulations, highlighting the ability of the model to capture the main thermofluid trends associated with mixing-controlled combustion. The results are used to discuss the sensitivity of the predicted flame structure to inter-zone transport assumptions and to identify the modelling requirements for extending multizone combustion approaches beyond predominantly premixed configurations. By addressing diffusion flames within a reduced-order multizone framework, this work contributes to the development of computationally efficient combustion models for thermofluid analysis, parametric studies and future coupling with higher-fidelity simulations or optimisation procedures.
title: Assessment of Multizone Combustion Modelling for Diffusion Flame Applications

description:
The Baja SAE Brazil competition challenges engineering students to design and build off-road vehicle prototypes capable of operating under severe terrain and load conditions. In this context, onboard electronics and telemetry systems play a fundamental role in monitoring vehicle performance, identifying failures, and supporting decision-making during testing and competitions.

In the prototype developed by the Cerrado Baja SAE team at the Federal University of Uberlândia (UFU), the monitoring of operational parameters was carried out in a predominantly reactive manner due to the absence of an integrated data acquisition and transmission system. To address this limitation, this work presents the development and integration of an onboard electronics and telemetry system applied to the team's vehicle.

The proposed system enables the monitoring of variables such as vehicle speed using a Hall-effect sensor, fuel level through analog sensing, engine and critical component temperatures, engine speed (RPM), and longitudinal acceleration. In addition, it includes the electronic activation of the brake light, the development of an emergency shutdown system (Kill Switch) with a reinforced mechanical structure, and a Multi-GNSS module for recording the vehicle's trajectory and traveled distance.

The collected data are processed by microcontrollers, displayed to the driver on a steering wheel-mounted display, and transmitted via wireless telemetry to a monitoring interface used by the technical team. Consequently, the system enhances the prototype's diagnostic capabilities, supports data-driven decision-making, and contributes to the integration of knowledge in automotive engineering, embedded electronics, and applied programming within an academic environment.

This research presents the development of a low-cost sound intensity probe by repurposing microphones and amplifiers acquired by the Federal University of Uberlândia that had become inactive due to technological obsolescence. Instead of replacing these devices with expensive commercial equipment, the project demonstrates how existing hardware can be reused to create a reliable measurement system for sound intensity analysis. The proposed solution combines digital signal processing techniques with electroacoustic principles to implement a complete and functional prototype suitable for research and educational purposes.

The probe was designed using a pair of microphones arranged in a face-to-face configuration, enabling the estimation of acoustic particle velocity through the pressure gradient method. A physical structure was also manufacture to assemble probes, cables and pre-amplificators. The implementation employed the Fahy method for sound intensity estimation, Welch spectral estimation to improve the robustness of frequency-domain analysis, and digital filtering techniques to reduce noise and enhance measurement accuracy. These methods were integrated into a complete data acquisition and processing framework capable of covering the entire audible frequency range.

To ensure the reliability of the developed system, acquisition and calibration procedures were established and validated based on the recommendations and according to the requirements of ISO 9614, the international standard for sound intensity measurements. The system's performance was evaluated analyzing the correlation between the microphone signals under different acoustic noise conditions, allowing the assessment of measurement consistency, signal quality, and overall accuracy. Experimental results demonstrated that the proposed prototype provides reliable sound intensity measurements while significantly reducing implementation costs compared with commercial instruments. The developed system therefore represents a practical and affordable alternative for laboratory experiments, engineering education, and academic research involving acoustic field characterization and sound intensity measurement.

description: The high costs of specialized acoustic instrumentation, such as impedance tubes, restrict experimental capabilities in academic acoustics and vibration laboratories. This paper presents the development and validation of an in-situ measurement methodology designed to leverage existing general-purpose laboratory assets in these facilities. The system determines the ensemble-averaged surface normal impedance and sound absorption coefficient (α) using Environmental Anonymous Noise (EA-Noise) excitation. The experimental hardware comprises two prepolarized free-field condenser microphones, a custom CAD holder manufactured via 3D printing to ensure precise transducer positioning, and a multi-channel data acquisition board connected to a computer running a digital signal processing algorithm implemented in MATLAB®. The processing routine incorporates a switching technique for phase mismatch correction and a critical coherence criterion ($\gamma^2_{\text{crit}} > 0.9$) to reject transient disturbances. Validation experiments were performed on rock wool (0.10 m) and glass wool (0.05 m) samples under four scenarios: simulated industrial noise, pink noise, laboratory ambient noise, and outdoor urban traffic. Results showed a systematic underestimation of the sound absorption coefficient. The highest metrological agreement with reference data was achieved under simulated industrial noise, yielding a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 25.21% for rock wool and 25.24% for glass wool, due to higher temporal energy density and spectral entropy. Crucially, excluding mathematically unstable low-frequency bands, specifically the 125 Hz band for rock wool, and both the 125 Hz and 250 Hz bands for glass wool, significantly reduced measurement errors, lowering the respective MAPE values to 18.07% and 16.34%. Identified limitations include edge effects on the smaller glass wool sample and wind-induced vibrations outdoors. Reaching an estimated Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of 3 to 4, this implementation provides academic acoustics and vibration laboratories with a viable alternative for specialized acoustic characterization without dedicated commercial hardware.
title: Environmental Anonymous Noise-Based In-Situ Sound Absorption Characterization Using Standard Laboratory Assets

description:
The technological development of humanity is intrinsically tied to growing energy consumption, and as global demand has intensified, finding new routes for renewable fuel production, or improving those already available, has become increasingly urgent. Fixed-bed pyrolysis of forest residue biomass, such as Eucalyptus grandis woodchips, is a very promising option due to its capacity to sequester carbon. One practical difficulty in modeling this phenomenon is that the dense, macroscopic particle beds typical of woodchip reactors cause Lagrangian–Discrete Element Method (DEM) simulations to diverge, so an alternative Eulerian formulation was adopted.
This work develops a CFD model using the software Simcenter STAR-CCM+ to represent the pyrolysis of E. grandis woodchips at a laboratory-scale fixed-bed reactor at 800 °C. An Eulerian porous medium with Direct Yield Mapping (DYM) is used, in which devolatilisation yields obtained experimentally at the LCE+/UECE laboratory enter the domain as analytical source terms through Field Functions. The steady-state solver combines Segregated Flow with Realizable k–ε Two-Layer turbulence, Discrete Ordinates Method (DOM) radiation with participating media, and the Eddy Dissipation Concept (EDC) for turbulence–chemistry interaction. Gas-phase reactions are modelled in the reactor freeboard, comprising steam reforming of tar (C₇H₈), steam and dry reforming of methane, and the water-gas shift reaction (WGSR), the primary devolatilisation follows a first-order Arrhenius law.
The polyhedral mesh generated has 429,097 cells. Predicted dry-basis syngas compositions are compared with Gasboard-3100 measurements taken after gas washing and condensation, with a good agreement, with H₂ yield deviating by only +0.88 pp (+2.2%). These results validate the model as a good basis for investigating steam co-injection as an H₂ enrichment strategy.
title: CFD Modelling of Eucalyptus Woodchips Pyrolysis for Increased Renewable Hydrogen Production

description: Rolling bearings are among the most failure-prone components in rotating machinery, and accurate estimation of their Remaining Useful Life (RUL) is essential for predictive maintenance. While vibration-based diagnostics, such as envelope analysis, cepstrum and ISO 20816 velocity trending, are well established for mechanically induced defects associated with BPFO, BPFI, BSF and FTF, an emerging and less-instrumented degradation path is electrical bearing damage caused by circulating or induced currents in inverter-driven and electrified drivetrains, producing electrical discharge machining (EDM) and fritting that often precede measurable vibration growth. Few accelerated-life test benches combine synchronised electrical and bidirectional vibration diagnostics tailored to RUL modelling. This work reports preliminary evidence from a small-scale rig operating at approximately 15 Hz (900 rpm) that forces a controlled current (~1.5 A) through a grease-lubricated, mechanically loaded bearing, and proposes its evolution into a dedicated RUL test bench. Horizontal (X) and vertical (Z) accelerometers, an oscilloscope and a temperature sensor were monitored over a ten-day window, with signals processed using RMS, crest factor, kurtosis, envelope demodulation, cepstrum and power spectral density. Results show intermittent current with alternating high- and low-impedance states, consistent with mixed EDM/fritting conduction. The vertical axis exhibited markedly higher peaks, kurtosis and envelope energy, indicating a localised impulsive source within the loaded zone, whereas the horizontal axis showed dominant overall velocity growth and sharper once-per-revolution cepstral coherence, reflecting the global structural response; velocity RMS increased by 44% (X) and 60% (Z) over ten days. Spectral energy converged to approximately 10.6 m/s² on both axes, sharing a resonance band near 700–850 Hz. These directional, multi-domain signatures support the design of a fully instrumented bench with synchronised current, voltage, bidirectional vibration and tachometer acquisition, controlled current levels and post-test inspection, establishing a reproducible platform for physics-informed RUL prognostic models for bearings under combined electrical and mechanical loading.

description: Large-Scale Additive Manufacturing (LSAM) has emerged as a transformative manufacturing technology for producing large-format polymer components with reduced material waste, shorter development cycles and enhanced design flexibility. The increasing industrial implementation of LSAM has intensified the need for reliable methodologies capable of efficiently characterizing both dimensional and geometric quality of these additive-manufactured components. Even though geometric integrity is a key requirement for the industrial deployment of LSAM technologies, the assessment of such manufactured components is often limited to discrete dimensional measurements, which provide only a partial representation of the manufacturing process's geometric response. To contribute to an improved integral characterization of LSAM-produced parts, this paper introduces an exploratory framework that combines digital geometric acquisition with comparative analysis against the nominal digital model, thereby enabling the identification, visualization, and discussion of deviation patterns across the entire component geometry. The resulting information is analyzed to establish meaningful descriptors of manufacturing behavior and geometric fidelity. Rather than just proposing acceptance criteria or process improvement strategies, the framework seeks to demonstrate the value of digital geometric characterization as a research methodology for understanding process capability and supporting future developments in qualification procedures, product design and sustainable manufacturing.
title: An Exploratory Framework for Geometric Characterization in Large-Scale Additive Manufacturing

description:
Renewable Energy Communities (RECs) have become a key instrument in the European energy transition, promoting decentralised renewable generation, local energy sharing, and the active participation of citizens, small and medium-sized enterprises, and public authorities. This paper presents a regulatory and implementation-focused analysis of RECs, examining how the European framework has been transposed into the Portuguese legal, institutional, and operational context.
The study reviews the main principles that define RECs, including open and voluntary participation, autonomy, effective control, geographical proximity, and the prioritisation of environmental, economic, and social benefits over profit maximisation. It also clarifies the distinctions between Renewable Energy Communities, Citizen Energy Communities, and collective self-consumption schemes, which are frequently treated as equivalent despite their distinct legal and organisational characteristics.
Drawing on regulatory analysis and practical implementation experience, the paper proposes a structured and replicable workflow for establishing a REC in Portugal. The proposed approach covers the main stages of the process, from the preliminary assessment of local generation and consumption conditions to governance design, technical certification, participant registration, energy-sharing mechanisms, and operational deployment.
The framework is illustrated through real-world implementation examples in Portugal and supported by a comparative analysis involving selected European countries. This comparison highlights differences in regulatory maturity, administrative procedures, institutional coordination, and adoption levels. The analysis identifies persistent challenges, including administrative complexity, the interpretation of proximity requirements, stakeholder coordination, member integration and withdrawal, and the allocation of responsibilities among the entities involved. Particular attention is given to barriers that may hinder or delay successful project implementation.
The main contribution of this work is the development of a practical, structured, and reproducible framework that bridges the gap between regulatory requirements and implementation needs in the Portuguese context. The proposed approach may support policymakers, community promoters, public authorities, energy companies, and other stakeholders in the design and implementation of Renewable Energy Communities in Portugal.

description: The in-situ production of biochar from agricultural and forestry residues offers a sustainable pathway to recover and improve soil quality. This ongoing work details the design methodology for a small-scale, continuous autothermic biochar pyrolyzer. The reactor operates by utilizing the heat generated from the biomass itself, combining a low-oxygen primary blanket combustion and a secondary combustion of volatile gases in separated side chambers. To establish the reactor's foundational geometry—an irregular pentagonal prism acting as an elongated hopper—an analytical thermo-kinetic model was developed based on the properties of shredded Pinus pinaster. This analytical framework evaluates system-wide mass and energy balances, incorporating an empirical gasification model to estimate syngas composition and determine heating values. System thermal efficiency is addressed through a heat resistance network, accounting for internal sensible heat, moisture evaporation, and external heat losses via natural convection and radiation. Furthermore, a jet pump mechanism is characterized to act as the primary pressure-control element, regulating the motive flow and suction pressure to match the system's precise oxidant requirements. Ongoing improvements to the system model include incorporating environmental radiation gains, dynamic surface temperature calculations based on varying insulation properties, and adjusted mixed-gas densities. This integrated analytical approach aims to deliver a robust design for in-situ biochar production.
